'''Purée Mongole''', also called '''Cream Mongole''', is a creamed [[split pea]]-tomato soup of unknown origin; a recipe for it was printed in 1889.<ref>Alessandro Filippini, 1889. ''The Table: How to Buy Food, How to Cook It, an How to Serve It'' (New York: Charles L. Webster) p 158; [http://www.barrypopik.com/index.php/new_york_city/entry/mongole_soup_potage_mongole_puree_mongole_creme_mongole quoted on-line, with other vintage recipes].</ref> Popular during the period between the 1920s–1940s, it is similar to Boula which is made with [[turtle soup]].<ref name=lovegren>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fZIRc28P5xYC&q=mongole&pg=PT88 |title=Fashionable Food: Seven Decades of Food Fads |author=Sylvia Lovegren |publisher=University of Chicago Press |year=2005 |isbn=0-226-49407-1 |pages=77–78 |access-date=2008-09-11 }}</ref>

Purée Mongole is usually made with [[carrot]]s, [[onion]]s, white [[turnip]]s, [[leek]]s, a stock (either beef or chicken) and milk. Depending on the recipe, it can have [[Julienning|julienne]] carrots and be seasoned with [[curry powder]],  ground cloves, [[turmeric]], nutmeg, [[cumin]], and basil, in addition to salt and pepper.<ref name=table>{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/tablehowtobuyfo00filigoog |quote=Purée Mongole -wiki. |title=The Table: How to Buy Food, how to Cook It, and how to Serve it |author=Alexander Filippini |publisher=C. L. Webster & company |year=1889 |page=[https://archive.org/details/tablehowtobuyfo00filigoog/page/n173 158] |access-date=2008-09-11}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.privatelabelcookingebooks.com/free-recipes/index.php?cmd=recipe&cat=6&recipe=271 |title=Purée Mongole |publisher=privatelabelcookingebooks.com |date=2007-09-17 |access-date=2008-09-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110715113305/http://www.privatelabelcookingebooks.com/free-recipes/index.php?cmd=recipe&cat=6&recipe=271 |archive-date=2011-07-15 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Simplified recipes printed in many vintage cookbooks, including the 1946 edition of the ''[[Joy of Cooking]]'', used canned, condensed pea and tomato soups as a base with additional vegetables and seasonings.<ref name=lovegren/>
